```{python}
#| label: c04-setup
#| code-summary: "Chapter setup"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from mdmx import artifacts, hooi, latex, lifetable, plotting, provenance, smoothing
from mdmx import tensor as tz
from mdmx.config import params

provenance.start_chapter("04-tucker")
plotting.use_style()
P = params()
T = artifacts.load("tensor")
M, observed = T["M"], T["observed"]
S, A, C, Tn = M.shape
years, pops, names = T["years"], T["pops"], T["pop_names"]
obs4 = np.broadcast_to(observed[None, None], M.shape)
Mz = np.nan_to_num(M)            # unobserved cells are never read, but must be numbers
```

## What the decomposition is for

The decomposition has two jobs (paper §3).  The first is to find a **shared
basis** in which every mortality schedule can be written: a sex factor
matrix $\mathbf{S}$ ($2 \times r_1$) and an age factor matrix $\mathbf{A}$
($110 \times r_2$) that are the same for every population and every year.
Writing each schedule in that common basis gives every output of the
system — model life tables, fitted schedules, predictions, forecasts — what
we call *shared-basis coherence*: both sexes' schedules are combinations of
the same age patterns.  The basis itself does not tie the two sexes together
(with $r_1 = 2$ the sex factor imposes nothing; see below); they are tied by
the low-rank models built on the cores downstream, such as the forecasters'
few principal components and the regimes' deviations.  The coordinates of a country-year's
schedule in the basis form its **effective core**, the $r_1 \times r_2$
matrix

$$
\mathcal{G}_{c,t} \;=\; \mathbf{S}^{\top}\, \mathcal{M}_{c,t}\, \mathbf{A},
\qquad\text{so that}\qquad
\mathcal{M}_{c,t} \;\approx\; \mathbf{S}\, \mathcal{G}_{c,t}\, \mathbf{A}^{\top}
$$

where $\mathcal{M}_{c,t}$ is the $2 \times 110$ matrix of
$\operatorname{logit}(q_x)$ for population $c$ in year $t$.  Every later
chapter works with these effective cores.

The second job is to describe how mortality varies **across populations
and over time** — the country and year modes of the tensor — and, in doing
so, to say something about the country-years for which we have no
(non-exceptional) data.  That is a *completion* problem: about 70% of the
country-year cells are unobserved.

The two jobs are done in turn, so that values filled in for the unobserved
country-years never shape the basis or the cores of the observed ones.  The
sex and age bases are estimated from observed schedules only, which needs
no imputation, and every observed country-year is represented by its exact
projection on that basis (steps 1–3).  The unobserved country-years are
then filled by a low-rank model of the country and year modes, fitted to
observed data only by EM, with its ranks chosen by out-of-sample prediction
(step 4).

## Step 1 — the shared sex and age bases

Each observed country-year contributes one complete $2 \times 110$ schedule.
Stacking those schedules side by side gives the age unfolding
$\mathbf{M}_{(2)}$ ($110 \times 2N_{\text{obs}}$) and the sex unfolding
$\mathbf{M}_{(1)}$ ($2 \times 110 N_{\text{obs}}$) of the *observed* data,
with no gaps.  Their left singular vectors are the factor matrices
(the paper's shared bases, §3.2).  The sex mode has only two levels and is kept at full rank,
$r_1 = 2$.  The age rank $r_2$ is the smallest number of components that
captures a share $\tau =$ `{python} P.tucker.tau` of the variance of
$\mathbf{M}_{(2)}$ (the paper's rank rule, in §3.2).  Computing an SVD of a $110 \times 9{,}000$
matrix is quick; we use the equivalent eigen-decomposition of the
$110 \times 110$ matrix $\mathbf{M}_{(2)} \mathbf{M}_{(2)}^\top$
(`mdmx.tensor.leading_left_vectors`).  Singular vectors are only defined up
to sign; `mdmx.tensor.fix_signs` makes the largest entry of each positive so
that results are identical on every computer.  The first age vector is then
turned, where needed, to point the same way as the mean observed schedule, so
that it has the shape of a $\operatorname{logit}(q_x)$ schedule (negative at almost every
age) and its core entry rises as mortality falls.

```{python}
#| label: c04-bases
#| code-summary: "Estimate the shared sex and age bases from observed schedules (cached)"
def _bases():
    return tz.sex_age_bases(Mz, observed, tau=P.tucker.tau,
                            age_bounds=tuple(P.tucker.age_rank_bounds))

bases = artifacts.stage("tucker_bases", _bases, inputs=["tensor"], params=P.section("tucker"),
                        code=[_bases, tz.sex_age_bases, tz.leading_left_vectors, tz.select_rank,
                              tz.fix_signs], desc="Shared sex and age bases from observed schedules")
U_sex, U_age_raw = bases["U_sex"], bases["U_age"]
latex.report("tuckerTau", P.tucker.tau, text=f"{P.tucker.tau:g}", desc="Variance share tau of the rank rule for r2")
r1, r2 = U_sex.shape[1], U_age_raw.shape[1]
print(f"r1 (sex) = {r1}, r2 (age) = {r2}")
print(f"Variance of the age unfolding captured by {r2} components: {bases['cumvar_age'][r2 - 1]:.6f}")
print("Sex factor matrix S (rows: female, male):")
print(np.round(U_sex, 3))
latex.report("tuckerRankSex", r1, desc="Sex rank r1")
latex.report("tuckerRankAge", r2, desc="Age rank r2 (tau rule on observed schedules)")
latex.report("tuckerVarAge", 100 * bases["cumvar_age"][r2 - 1], digits=3,
             desc="Percent of age-unfolding variance captured by r2 components")
latex.report("tuckerVarAgeFirst", 100 * bases["cumvar_age"][0], digits=1,
             desc="Percent of age-unfolding variance captured by the first component")
```

The two columns of $\mathbf{S}$ have entries of the same sign (first column:
the average of the sexes) and of opposite sign (second column: the sex
difference).  Because $r_1 = 2 = S$, $\mathbf{S}$ is just a change of
coordinates between "female, male" and "average, difference"; the sex
structure of every schedule is carried by the effective cores, and its
*coherence* across the system comes from the shared age basis.

```{python}
#| label: fig-s4-sv-decay
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative share of variance captured by the leading components of the age unfolding of the observed schedules (left) and the singular values on a log scale (right). The dashed line marks τ = 0.9999 and the vertical line the selected age rank."
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
k = np.arange(1, len(bases["sigma_age"]) + 1)
ax1.plot(k, bases["cumvar_age"], marker="o", ms=2.5, color=plotting.COLORS["model"])
ax1.axhline(P.tucker.tau, ls="--", color="grey", lw=0.8)
ax1.axvline(r2, color=plotting.COLORS["highlight"], lw=1)
ax1.set_ylim(0.999, 1.00002)
ax1.set_xlabel("Number of age components"); ax1.set_ylabel("Cumulative variance share")
ax2.semilogy(k, bases["sigma_age"], marker="o", ms=2.5, color=plotting.COLORS["model"])
ax2.axvline(r2, color=plotting.COLORS["highlight"], lw=1)
ax2.set_xlabel("Component"); ax2.set_ylabel("Singular value")
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s4-sv-decay")
plt.show()
```

## Step 2 — smoothing the age basis

The leading age components are smooth, but the higher-order ones pick up
some single-year wiggle where the data are noisy.  Following paper §3.2,
each column except the first is smoothed with a Gaussian kernel whose width
grows with age, so that the infant peak, the childhood minimum and
the young-adult "accident hump" are smoothed lightly and the old-age tail
more strongly.  Components 2–5 have their own settings; all higher
components share one narrow, constant bandwidth.  Ages 0 and 1 are reset to
their unsmoothed values, and the basis is then re-orthonormalised (QR).
`mdmx.smoothing` implements the kernel as a matrix, so smoothing a column
is one matrix–vector product.

```{python}
#| label: c04-smooth
#| code-summary: "Smooth the age basis and re-orthonormalise (cached)"
def _smooth():
    U, diag = smoothing.smooth_age_basis(
        U_age_raw, P.tucker.smooth_components, P.tucker.smooth_rest_sigma,
        P.tucker.smooth_preserve, P.tucker.smooth_orth_tol)
    return {"U_age": U, "diagnostics": diag}

sm = artifacts.stage("tucker_age_smoothed", _smooth, inputs=["tucker_bases"],
                     params=P.section("tucker"), code=[_smooth, smoothing],
                     desc="Smoothed, orthonormal age basis")
U_age = sm["U_age"]
for k_, v_ in sm["diagnostics"].items():
    print(f"{k_:>28s}: {v_:.2e}")
latex.report("tuckerQRMaxChange", sm["diagnostics"]["max_change_preserved_ages"], digits=3,
             desc="Largest change at ages 0-1 caused by re-orthonormalisation")
latex.report("tuckerSmoothOwnLast", 1 + len(P.tucker.smooth_components),
             desc="Last age component with a bandwidth of its own (components 2 to it; later ones share one)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-s4-age-basis
#| fig-cap: "The first six age basis functions (columns of A) after smoothing (solid) and before (thin grey). The first is close to the mean logit(q_x) schedule; each later one changes sign and rebalances mortality between age groups."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(11, 6), sharex=True)
ages = T["ages"]
crossings = {}
for k_, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    ax.plot(ages, U_age_raw[:, k_], color="#bbbbbb", lw=0.8)
    ax.plot(ages, U_age[:, k_], color=plotting.COLORS["model"], lw=1.5)
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.5)
    ax.set_title(f"Component {k_ + 1}", fontsize=10)
    sgn = np.sign(U_age[1:, k_])
    crossings[k_ + 1] = [int(a) for a in ages[1:][np.flatnonzero(np.diff(sgn) != 0) + 1]]
for ax in axes[1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("Age")
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s4-age-basis")
plt.show()
print("Ages (≥1) at which each component changes sign:", crossings)
if crossings[2]:
    latex.report("tuckerAgeTwoCrossing", crossings[2][0], text=str(crossings[2][0]),
                 desc="Age at which the second age component first changes sign")
```

## Step 3 — the effective cores of the observed country-years

With $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{A}$ fixed, the effective core of each
observed country-year is a projection, $\mathcal{G}_{c,t} =
\mathbf{S}^\top \mathcal{M}_{c,t}\mathbf{A}$, and the schedule implied by
it is $\hat{\mathcal{M}}_{c,t} = \mathbf{S}\mathcal{G}_{c,t}\mathbf{A}^\top$.
The only approximation is the truncation of the age basis to $r_2$
components, so the reconstruction of observed data is very close.

```{python}
#| label: c04-cores
#| code-summary: "Project every observed schedule onto the shared basis; measure the fit"
Y_obs = tz.effective_cores(Mz, observed, U_sex, U_age)            # (r1, r2, C, T), NaN if unobserved
M_rec = tz.schedules_from_cores(np.nan_to_num(Y_obs), U_sex, U_age)
err = (M_rec - Mz)[obs4]
r2_obs = 1 - np.sum(err ** 2) / np.sum((Mz[obs4] - Mz[obs4].mean()) ** 2)
rel_err = np.linalg.norm(err) / np.linalg.norm(Mz[obs4])
e0_obs = lifetable.e0_from_logit(np.moveaxis(Mz, 1, -1))[:, observed]
e0_rec = lifetable.e0_from_logit(np.moveaxis(M_rec, 1, -1))[:, observed]
de0 = np.abs(e0_rec - e0_obs)
print(f"Observed cells: RMSE {np.sqrt(np.mean(err ** 2)):.4f}, R² {r2_obs:.6f}, "
      f"relative error {rel_err:.4f}")
print(f"|Δe0| between observed and reconstructed schedules: mean {de0.mean():.3f}, max {de0.max():.3f} years")
latex.report("tuckerObsRMSE", float(np.sqrt(np.mean(err ** 2))), digits=3, desc="RMSE (logit) on observed cells")
latex.report("tuckerObsRsq", float(r2_obs), digits=5, desc="R-squared on observed cells")
latex.report("tuckerObsRelErr", float(rel_err), digits=4, desc="Relative Frobenius error on observed cells")
latex.report("tuckerObsMeanAbsDeZero", float(de0.mean()), digits=3, desc="Mean |delta e0|, observed vs reconstructed")
latex.report("tuckerObsMaxAbsDeZero", float(de0.max()), digits=2, desc="Max |delta e0|, observed vs reconstructed")
```

## Step 4 — completing the unobserved country-years

To describe the country and year modes, and to say what the model implies
for country-years without baseline data, we fit a Tucker model to the
effective cores in which the country and year modes are compressed to ranks
$r_3$ and $r_4$:

$$
\mathcal{G}_{c,t} \;\approx\; \mathcal{G} \times_3 \mathbf{c}_c^\top \times_4 \mathbf{t}_t^\top ,
$$

with $\mathbf{C}$ ($C \times r_3$) and $\mathbf{T}$ ($T \times r_4$)
orthonormal.  It is fitted to observed country-years only, by the EM
algorithm (`mdmx.tensor.complete_cores`): start with the country means
of the observed cores, fit the model, replace *only* the unobserved slices by the
fit, and repeat until the filled values stop changing.  At convergence the
observed slices are data, the unobserved slices are the model's own
prediction, and the factors are those of the completed array — so the made-
up values exert no pull of their own.  One limit follows: a calendar year in
which *no* population is observed — every year of the influenza pandemics and
of COVID-19, for example, is exceptional in every population with data — gives
its year loading nothing to be estimated from, so EM leaves it close to where
it started and the model returns roughly each country's mean schedule there
(for Sweden the same e₀ in 1918 as in each of 2020–22; chapter 08).  The model's values
in such years are not predictions; chapter 08 builds the baselines of
exceptional years differently.

### Choosing the ranks by prediction

A variance threshold cannot choose $r_3$ and $r_4$ here: most of the array
is missing, and the share of variance a component "explains" depends on how
the gaps were filled.  Instead we ask how well each candidate pair predicts
data it has not seen.  A random `{python} f"{100 * P.tucker.holdout_share:.0f}"`% of the
observed country-years is hidden, the model is fitted to the rest, and the
hidden schedules are predicted.

```{python}
#| label: c04-rank-search
#| code-summary: "Hold-out search over the completion ranks (cached; a few minutes)"
grid = [(rc, rt) for rc in P.tucker.completion_country_ranks for rt in P.tucker.completion_year_ranks]

def _loss(Y_completed, hidden):
    rec = tz.schedules_from_cores(Y_completed, U_sex, U_age)
    h4 = np.broadcast_to(hidden[None, None], M.shape)
    e0p = lifetable.e0_from_logit(np.moveaxis(rec, 1, -1))[:, hidden]
    e0t = lifetable.e0_from_logit(np.moveaxis(Mz, 1, -1))[:, hidden]
    return {"rmse": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((rec[h4] - Mz[h4]) ** 2))),
            "e0_mae": float(np.mean(np.abs(e0p - e0t)))}

def _search():
    rows = tz.holdout_rank_search(Y_obs, observed, grid, share=P.tucker.holdout_share,
                                  seed=P.tucker.holdout_seed, max_iter=P.tucker.search_max_iter,
                                  tol=P.tucker.em_tol, loss=_loss)
    # Country-mean imputation, a naive benchmark, on the same hidden cells.
    rows.append({"r_country": 0, "r_year": 0, "iterations": 0,
                 **_loss(tz.country_mean_impute(np.nan_to_num(Y_obs), observed & ~_hidden()), _hidden())})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def _hidden():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(P.tucker.holdout_seed)
    ci, ti = np.nonzero(observed)
    pick = rng.choice(len(ci), size=max(1, int(round(P.tucker.holdout_share * len(ci)))), replace=False)
    h = np.zeros_like(observed); h[ci[pick], ti[pick]] = True
    return h

search = artifacts.stage("tucker_rank_search", _search, inputs=["tucker_bases", "tucker_age_smoothed", "tensor"],
                         params=P.section("tucker"),
                         code=[_search, _loss, _hidden, tz.complete_cores, tz.holdout_rank_search],
                         desc="Hold-out prediction error of the completion model by rank")
cand = search[search["r_country"] > 0]
best = cand.loc[cand["rmse"].idxmin()]
ref = search[search["r_country"] == 0].iloc[0]
r3, r4 = int(best["r_country"]), int(best["r_year"])
print(cand.pivot(index="r_country", columns="r_year", values="rmse").round(3))
print(f"\nSelected ranks: r3 = {r3}, r4 = {r4}  (hold-out RMSE {best['rmse']:.3f}, e0 MAE {best['e0_mae']:.2f} y)")
print(f"Country-mean imputation on the same cells: RMSE {ref['rmse']:.3f}, e0 MAE {ref['e0_mae']:.2f} y")
latex.report("tuckerRankCountry", r3, desc="Country rank r3 of the completion model (hold-out)")
latex.report("tuckerRankYear", r4, desc="Year rank r4 of the completion model (hold-out)")
latex.report("tuckerHoldRMSE", float(best["rmse"]), digits=3, desc="Hold-out RMSE (logit), selected completion model")
latex.report("tuckerHoldMAE", float(best["e0_mae"]), digits=2, desc="Hold-out e0 MAE (years), selected completion model")
latex.report("tuckerHoldRMSEMean", float(ref["rmse"]), digits=3, desc="Hold-out RMSE, country-mean imputation")
latex.report("tuckerHoldMAEMean", float(ref["e0_mae"]), digits=2, desc="Hold-out e0 MAE, country-mean imputation")
latex.report("tuckerHoldN", int(_hidden().sum()), desc="Country-years hidden in the rank search")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-s4-rank-search
#| fig-cap: "Hold-out prediction error of the completion model for each pair of country and year ranks: RMSE of logit(q_x) (left) and mean absolute error of e0 (right) on the hidden country-years. The selected pair is outlined; country-mean imputation (EM's starting values) gives the values in the titles."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
for ax, col, lab in zip(axes, ["rmse", "e0_mae"], ["RMSE, logit$(q_x)$", "MAE, $e_0$ (years)"]):
    piv = cand.pivot(index="r_country", columns="r_year", values=col)
    im = ax.imshow(piv.to_numpy(), cmap="viridis_r", aspect="auto")
    ax.set_xticks(range(piv.shape[1]), piv.columns); ax.set_yticks(range(piv.shape[0]), piv.index)
    ax.set_xlabel("Year rank $r_4$"); ax.set_ylabel("Country rank $r_3$"); ax.grid(False)
    for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(piv.to_numpy()):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color="white")
    bi, bj = list(piv.index).index(r3), list(piv.columns).index(r4)
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((bj - 0.5, bi - 0.5), 1, 1, fill=False, ec="red", lw=2))
    ax.set_title(f"{lab}; country means: {ref[col]:.2f}", fontsize=9)
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s4-rank-search")
plt.show()
```

### The final completion model

```{python}
#| label: c04-complete
#| code-summary: "Fit the completion model at the selected ranks (cached)"
def _complete():
    Yc, (U_c, U_t), core, hist = tz.complete_cores(Y_obs, observed, r3, r4,
                                                   max_iter=P.tucker.em_max_iter, tol=P.tucker.em_tol)
    return {"G_ct": Yc, "U_country": U_c, "U_year": U_t, "core": core,
            "history": pd.DataFrame(hist)}

comp = artifacts.stage("tucker_completion", _complete, inputs=["tucker_rank_search", "tucker_bases", "tucker_age_smoothed", "tensor"],
                       params={**P.section("tucker"), "r3": r3, "r4": r4},
                       code=[_complete, tz.complete_cores],
                       desc="Completion model: country and year factors, core, completed effective cores")
hist = comp["history"]
print(f"EM iterations: {len(hist)}; final relative change {hist['rel_change'].iloc[-1]:.1e}")
latex.report("tuckerEMIterations", len(hist), desc="EM iterations of the final completion model")


def _sci(x: float) -> str:
    """x as a power of ten in text-mode LaTeX, e.g. $5.5 \\times 10^{-5}$ (not for use inside math)."""
    mantissa, exponent = f"{x:.1e}".split("e")
    power = f"10^{{{int(exponent)}}}"
    return f"${power}$" if mantissa == "1.0" else f"${mantissa} \\times {power}$"


latex.report("tuckerEMTol", P.tucker.em_tol, text=_sci(P.tucker.em_tol),
             desc="EM tolerance: relative change of the filled values")
latex.report("tuckerEMFinalChange", float(hist["rel_change"].iloc[-1]), text=_sci(float(hist["rel_change"].iloc[-1])),
             desc="Relative change of the filled values at the last EM iteration")
```

### The HOSVD or higher-order orthogonal iteration

Each iteration of the completion model computes $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{T}$ by a truncated
HOSVD of the filled array: the leading left singular vectors of its country and year unfoldings.
A truncated HOSVD is quasi-optimal, not optimal.  Its squared error is at most the sum, over the
truncated modes, of the squared singular values each one discards, so with two modes truncated its
error is at most $\sqrt{2}$ times that of the best approximation with the same ranks.
Higher-order orthogonal iteration can come closer to the best: it updates each factor matrix in
turn, given the other, by least squares.  To see whether that would serve the completion model
better, the same EM is fitted with one sweep of it in place of the HOSVD at every iteration
(`mdmx.hooi.complete_cores_hooi`), at the selected ranks and with the same settings, and the two are
compared twice: by the residual of the observed cores after the final model's
`{python} f"{P.tucker.em_max_iter:,}"` iterations, and by how well they predict hidden country-years.
The second comparison uses `{python} P.section("checks")["hooi_splits"]` random splits, each hiding
`{python} f"{100 * P.tucker.holdout_share:.0f}"`% of the observed country-years as the rank search
does, drawn with their own seed rather than the one whose split chose the ranks.

```{python}
#| label: c04-hooi
#| code-summary: "The completion model with higher-order orthogonal iteration (cached; about a minute)"
CK = P.section("checks")


def _hooi_check():
    done, fac, core, hist = hooi.complete_cores_hooi(Y_obs, observed, r3, r4,
                                                     max_iter=P.tucker.em_max_iter, tol=P.tucker.em_tol)
    fit = pd.DataFrame({
        "method": ["HOSVD", "HOOI"],
        "resid_obs": [hooi.observed_residual(comp["G_ct"], observed, [comp["U_country"], comp["U_year"]],
                                             comp["core"]),
                      hooi.observed_residual(done, observed, fac, core)],
        "iterations": [len(comp["history"]), len(hist)]})
    rng = np.random.default_rng(CK["hooi_seed"])
    ci, ti = np.nonzero(observed)
    rows = []
    for split in range(CK["hooi_splits"]):
        pick = rng.choice(len(ci), size=max(1, int(round(P.tucker.holdout_share * len(ci)))), replace=False)
        hidden = np.zeros_like(observed)
        hidden[ci[pick], ti[pick]] = True
        for name, complete in (("HOSVD", tz.complete_cores), ("HOOI", hooi.complete_cores_hooi)):
            Yc = complete(Y_obs, observed & ~hidden, r3, r4, max_iter=P.tucker.search_max_iter,
                          tol=P.tucker.em_tol)[0]
            rows.append({"split": split + 1, "method": name, **_loss(Yc, hidden)})
    return {"fit": fit, "holdout": pd.DataFrame(rows)}


hc = artifacts.stage("tucker_hooi_check", _hooi_check,
                     inputs=["tensor", "tucker_bases", "tucker_age_smoothed", "tucker_completion"],
                     params={"r3": r3, "r4": r4, "em_max_iter": P.tucker.em_max_iter,
                             "search_max_iter": P.tucker.search_max_iter, "em_tol": P.tucker.em_tol,
                             "holdout_share": P.tucker.holdout_share, "splits": CK["hooi_splits"],
                             "seed": CK["hooi_seed"]},
                     code=[_hooi_check, _loss, hooi.complete_cores_hooi, hooi.observed_residual,
                           tz.complete_cores],
                     desc="The completion model with higher-order orthogonal iteration in place of the HOSVD: "
                          "fit to the observed cores and prediction of hidden country-years")
res = hc["fit"].set_index("method")["resid_obs"]
hooi_gain = 100 * (1 - res["HOOI"] / res["HOSVD"])
ho = hc["holdout"].pivot(index="split", columns="method", values=["rmse", "e0_mae"])
hooi_worse = int((ho[("rmse", "HOOI")] > ho[("rmse", "HOSVD")]).sum())
hooi_worse_e0 = int((ho[("e0_mae", "HOOI")] > ho[("e0_mae", "HOSVD")]).sum())
mean = ho.mean()
print(f"Residual of the observed cores: HOSVD {res['HOSVD']:.2f}, HOOI {res['HOOI']:.2f} ({hooi_gain:.1f} % lower)")
print(f"Hold-out, mean of {CK['hooi_splits']} splits: RMSE HOSVD {mean[('rmse', 'HOSVD')]:.3f}, "
      f"HOOI {mean[('rmse', 'HOOI')]:.3f} (HOOI worse in {hooi_worse}); e0 MAE HOSVD "
      f"{mean[('e0_mae', 'HOSVD')]:.2f}, HOOI {mean[('e0_mae', 'HOOI')]:.2f} y (HOOI worse in {hooi_worse_e0})")
latex.report("tuckerHOOIResidGain", hooi_gain, digits=1,
             desc="Residual of the observed cores, % lower with higher-order orthogonal iteration than with the HOSVD")
latex.report("tuckerHOSVDHoldRMSE", float(mean[("rmse", "HOSVD")]), digits=3,
             desc="Hold-out RMSE (logit), completion model with the HOSVD, mean of the random splits")
latex.report("tuckerHOOIHoldRMSE", float(mean[("rmse", "HOOI")]), digits=3,
             desc="Hold-out RMSE (logit), completion model with higher-order orthogonal iteration, mean of the splits")
latex.report("tuckerHOSVDHoldMAE", float(mean[("e0_mae", "HOSVD")]), digits=2,
             desc="Hold-out e0 MAE (years), completion model with the HOSVD, mean of the random splits")
latex.report("tuckerHOOIHoldMAE", float(mean[("e0_mae", "HOOI")]), digits=2,
             desc="Hold-out e0 MAE (years), completion model with higher-order orthogonal iteration, mean of the splits")
latex.report("tuckerHOOIWorseSplits", hooi_worse, desc="Random splits in which HOOI's hold-out RMSE is higher")
latex.report("tuckerHOOIWorseSplitsMAE", hooi_worse_e0, desc="Random splits in which HOOI's hold-out e0 MAE is higher")
latex.report("tuckerHOOISplits", int(CK["hooi_splits"]), desc="Random hold-out splits of the HOSVD/HOOI comparison")
ho.round(3)
```

Higher-order orthogonal iteration fits the observed cores more closely, as it must: one sweep never
moves the model away from the filled array, so the residual of the observed cores cannot rise from
one iteration to the next.  The closer fit does not carry over to country-years the model has not
seen: in `{python} hooi_worse` of the `{python} CK["hooi_splits"]` splits it predicts them less
well than the HOSVD.  The completion model keeps the HOSVD, which also keeps each iteration in
closed form.

## The decomposition artefact

Everything later chapters need is saved as one artefact, `tucker`:

* `U_sex`, `U_age` — the shared bases ($\mathbf{S}$, smoothed $\mathbf{A}$);
* `G_ct` — the effective core of **every** country-year: the exact projection
  where observed, the completion model's prediction elsewhere;
* `observed` — which country-years are data;
* `U_country`, `U_year`, `core` — the completion model.

```{python}
#| label: c04-save
#| code-summary: "Assemble and save the decomposition"
G_ct = np.where(observed[None, None], np.nan_to_num(Y_obs), comp["G_ct"])
tucker = artifacts.stage(
    "tucker",
    lambda: {"U_sex": U_sex, "U_age": U_age, "U_age_raw": U_age_raw, "G_ct": G_ct,
             "observed": observed, "U_country": comp["U_country"], "U_year": comp["U_year"],
             "core": comp["core"], "ranks": np.array([r1, r2, r3, r4]),
             "pops": pops, "years": years, "ages": T["ages"]},
    inputs=["tensor", "tucker_bases", "tucker_age_smoothed", "tucker_completion"],
    params=P.section("tucker"), desc="The MDMx decomposition used by every later chapter")
M_hat = tz.schedules_from_cores(tucker["G_ct"], tucker["U_sex"], tucker["U_age"])   # (S, A, C, T)
```

```{python}

    "Mode": ["Sex", "Age", "Country", "Year"],
    "Size": [S, A, C, Tn],
    "Rank": [r1, r2, r3, r4],

                  "hold-out prediction (completion model)", "hold-out prediction (completion model)"],
})
latex.save_table(ranks_tab, "tbl-s4-tucker-ranks", "Ranks of the decomposition.  The sex and age "
                 "bases are estimated from observed schedules; the country and year ranks are those "

                 escape_cells=False)
ranks_tab
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-s4-compression

n_obs_cells = int(obs4.sum())
n_param_basis = S * r1 + A * r2
n_param_cores = r1 * r2 * int(observed.sum())
fit_tab = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": ["Observed cells (data)", "Parameters: sex and age bases",
                 "Parameters: effective cores of observed country-years",

              f"{n_obs_cells / (n_param_basis + n_param_cores):.2f}",
              f"{np.sqrt(np.mean(err ** 2)):.3f}", f"{r2_obs:.5f}", f"{de0.mean():.3f}",

fit_tab
```

## Interpreting the country and year modes

```{python}
#| label: fig-s4-loadings
#| fig-cap: "Factor loadings of the completion model. Left: populations on the first two country components. Right: the first three year components against calendar year."
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
Uc, Ut = tucker["U_country"], tucker["U_year"]
ax1.scatter(Uc[:, 0], Uc[:, 1], s=12, color=plotting.COLORS["model"])
for i, p in enumerate(pops):
    ax1.annotate(p, (Uc[i, 0], Uc[i, 1]), fontsize=6, alpha=0.8)
ax1.set_xlabel("Country component 1"); ax1.set_ylabel("Country component 2")
for k_ in range(3):
    ax2.plot(years, Ut[:, k_], lw=1.2, label=f"Year component {k_ + 1}")
ax2.set_xlabel("Year"); ax2.legend()
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s4-loadings")
plt.show()
```

## Reconstruction and completion, illustrated

```{python}
#| label: fig-s4-reconstruction
#| fig-cap: "Observed logit(q_x) (points) and the schedule implied by the effective core (line) for four country-years, females and males. Every observed country-year is represented by its exact projection on the shared basis; the RMSE of each panel is shown."
SHOW = [("SWE", 1900), ("JPN", 2000), ("USA", 1960), ("RUS", 1990)]
pidx = {p: i for i, p in enumerate(pops)}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 7), sharex=True)
for ax, (pop, yr) in zip(axes.flat, SHOW):
    c, t = pidx[pop], int(yr - years[0])
    for s, sex in enumerate(("female", "male")):
        ax.plot(T["ages"], Mz[s, :, c, t], ".", ms=2.5, color=plotting.COLORS[sex], alpha=0.6)
        ax.plot(T["ages"], M_hat[s, :, c, t], color=plotting.COLORS[sex], lw=1.2, label=sex.title())
    rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((M_hat[:, :, c, t] - Mz[:, :, c, t]) ** 2))
    ax.set_title(f"{names[c]} {yr} (RMSE {rmse:.3f}{'' if observed[c, t] else ', not observed'})", fontsize=9)
axes[0, 0].legend()
for ax in axes[1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("Age")
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s4-reconstruction")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-s3-imputation

Right: logit(q_50), females, for four populations — observed years (points) and the completion model's values for unobserved years (line), including the years before each series starts."
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.4]})
```
